messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Tariq Mansour is a 41-year-old single man of Lebanese descent who works the morning shift at a fast food restaurant in a mid-sized Midwestern city. He presented for an initial psychological evaluation reporting significant distress that had been building for well over a year, and his PCL-5 score of 64 placed him firmly in the severe range for post-traumatic stress.

The event that reorganised Tariq's inner life occurred on an ordinary weekday morning, shortly before 9 a.m., when he witnessed a violent altercation outside his previous workplace — a convenience store where he had been employed at the time. A disagreement between two men escalated with terrifying speed. There was shouting, then the sharp, percussive crack of a firearm discharged at close range, and Tariq, standing no more than fifteen feet away, watched one of the men collapse onto the pavement. The sound of the shot — sudden, enormous, filling the air — was the axis around which the entire experience seemed to turn. Tariq was not physically harmed, but he stood frozen for what felt like minutes, certain in those moments that he was about to die, that the violence would turn toward him next. The police arrived, there were more loud voices and radio static, and by the time Tariq was driven home that evening, something fundamental had shifted in how the world felt to him.

In the months that followed, Tariq found that the world had become a place that required constant monitoring. He had come to believe, in a way that felt entirely rational to him, that safety was not a general condition but a specific and fragile one — available only in a small number of places he had carefully identified and tested. His apartment, a particular corner booth at a diner two blocks away, and the back stockroom at work were the boundaries of what felt survivable. Everywhere else, his nervous system remained on a kind of standing alert. When he heard unexpected sounds — a car backfiring, a dropped tray, a customer raising their voice at the counter — the alarm that moved through him was immediate and physical, his body already bracing for impact before his mind could intervene. He was certain, in those moments, that something catastrophic was unfolding.

It is at work, in the clamour of the breakfast rush, that Tariq's symptoms press most insistently against his daily life. The restaurant is loud by nature — the hiss of the fryer, the clatter of metal trays, the sudden bark of a manager calling out an order. Any sharp or unexpected sound pulls Tariq's attention completely away from what he is doing and floods him with the same vigilance he felt on the morning of the shooting. When a supervisor corrects him — over a missed order, a timing error, anything — the critical tone triggers something that goes beyond ordinary embarrassment. His body reads the sharpness in a voice as the leading edge of danger, and within seconds he is scanning the room, heart elevated, convinced that the situation is about to deteriorate in some serious and undefined way. Similarly, mornings themselves have become laden. The pre-9 a.m. hours, when the light looks a certain way and the shift is just beginning, carry a weight that Tariq cannot fully explain to his coworkers. He simply knows that something bad happened at that hour, and his body has not forgotten.

When something at work takes longer than expected — a delivery that is late, a customer who lingers — Tariq finds himself assuming, almost automatically, that the delay signals something wrong. This low-level dread is present most of the day, exhausting in its constancy.

What finally brought Tariq to seek help was a conversation with his younger sister, who told him plainly that he had become a different person — withdrawn, unreachable, afraid. He did not disagree. What he is most afraid of, sitting in the intake room, is that there is no version of this that gets better. What he is hoping for, quietly, is to be proven wrong.
